newsitem.title: HUNGARY: IBM's Hungary storage unit to boost output.
newsitem.headline: IBM's Hungary storage unit to boost output.

text.p: IBM's Hungarian disk drive plant will become the company's biggest in Europe when it boosts output to three million drives in 1997, a company official said on Thursday.
"The output in 1997 will be aproximately triple of what we had in 1996," Hans Fehlinger, general manager of the plant that is part of IBM's Storage Systems Division, told Reuters.
With the three million units per year output, this will be IBM's largest disk drive factory in Europe, he said.
The $100 million Szekesfehervar plant was recently extended by a 24,000 sq m unit in addition to the existing 10,000 sq m plant, Fehlinger said.
Fehlinger said IBM decided to set up shop in Hungary as infrastructure, availability of workforce and the cost-competitive environment met their requirements.
"We wanted to be close to our customers and work in a cost-competitive environment," he said.
Fehlinger added that IBM's recent announcement it would build a disk drive factory in Thailand does not mean Hungary is becoming less attractive for the company.
"We had our criteria to be here, they had their criteria to be in southeast Asia, and they go along with each other. There was no competition," he said.
IBM has invested some $1.32 billion this year in its storage business.

The Hungarian plant, in which IBM's investment Fehlinger said is "about three-quarters of the total ($100 million)" assembles and tests 3.5-inch disk drives for desktop computers and 2.5-inch drives for mobile appliances.
The parts come from southeast Asia, Germany and Italy and the final product is exported, 40 percent of it to IBM's own PC companies and 60 percent to other manufacturers, Fehlinger said.
They currently employ some 700 to 750 people but the workforce will grow at aproximately the same rate as output capacity grows.
"We will crawl up to the neighborhood of 2,500 employees," Fehlinger added.
He said business figures are reported on a consolidated basis for IBM's entire storage division -- which has factories in Germany, Singapore, Japan, China, Mexico and the United States.
He said they only plan production one year ahead, thus could not give output estimates for after 1997 but said that once reached, they aim to at least keep the three million drives per year level.
IBM has not experienced logistics problems other western companies complain about in Hungary, he added.
"We are satisfied with what we are getting and we have no logistics problems specific to Hungary," Fehlinger said.
The industrial park on the outskirts of Szekesfehervar also hosts Ford, Matsushita and Philips companies.
